Original P16.5:
P16.5 (T5): Finite-energy equations for nonample positivity classes
Extend the equation theory to big or pseudoeﬀective nonample classes, specifying the psh cone,
reference singularity type, energy and total mass. At zero volume, the existing probability
normalization must be replaced rather than retained unchanged.

Complete unchanged mathematical family:

10     The general non-Archimedean Monge–Ampère equation
Active items: P16.1, P16.2, P16.3, P16.4, P16.5, P16.6, P16.7. Status: Open in the
residual scope.

10.1    Atomic targets
P16.1 (T5): Finite-energy equations on singular or unibranch varieties
Extend the ﬁnite-energy non-Archimedean Monge–Ampère operator and its existence-and-
uniqueness theorem to singular or unibranch varieties, replacing each use of smoothness in
compactness, envelopes, energy diﬀerentiation and comparison. State all retained polarization
and ﬁeld hypotheses.

P16.2 (T5): Proper nonprojective algebraizable equation theories
Construct an appropriate replacement positivity datum and the associated psh, ﬁnite-energy,
comparison and equation theory on proper nonprojective algebraizable spaces. A proper
algebraic scheme with an ample line bundle is already projective, so retaining that datum
while dropping projectivity is not a new case.

P16.3 (T5): Finite-energy equations in positive residue characteristic
Construct the required ﬁnite-energy operator and prove existence and uniqueness when the
original residue-characteristic restriction is removed. Replace the resolution, model-regularity
and envelope inputs wherever they are used rather than merely changing the standing ﬁeld
hypothesis.

P16.4 (T4): Finite-energy equations over arbitrary complete valued ﬁelds
Extend the operator and existence theorem to nondiscrete valuations and arbitrary complete
non-Archimedean ﬁelds outside the established invariant-toric, skeleton-supported endpoint.
A deﬁnition of the ﬁnite-energy space alone does not establish the operator or the equation.

P16.5 (T5): Finite-energy equations for nonample positivity classes
Extend the equation theory to big or pseudoeﬀective nonample classes, specifying the psh cone,
reference singularity type, energy and total mass. At zero volume, the existing probability
normalization must be replaced rather than retained unchanged.

P16.6 (T4): Arbitrary-support ﬁnite-energy measures
Prove the operator and existence-and-uniqueness theorem for arbitrary ﬁnite-energy measure
support beyond the known toric skeletal regime. Measures must satisfy the correct mass and
energy conditions. Do not reduce arbitrary support to a single skeleton or replace the genuine
Monge–Ampère measure by another inverse measure construction.

P16.7 (T5): Finite-energy equations on nonalgebraizable analytic spaces
Construct the ﬁnite-energy operator and its existence-and-uniqueness theory on genuinely
nonalgebraizable analytic spaces, with an explicit positivity datum and the necessary com-
pactness, envelope and comparison replacements.




                                              73

10.2    What constitutes a solution
For each axis, state the retained hypotheses and construct the ﬁnite-energy operator together
with the corresponding existence-and-uniqueness theorem. Specify the measure mass and
ﬁnite-energy condition, uniqueness modulo constants and the replacement inputs for com-
pactness, envelopes, energy diﬀerentiation and comparison. An endpoint solving a special
toric measure class does not remove a general axis.

10.3    Full statement and detailed state of the art
Problem 10.1. Extend the ﬁnite-energy existence and uniqueness theory for the NA Monge–
Ampère equation beyond the currently proved combinations of smoothness, projectivity,
residue characteristic, valuation, positivity class, support, and algebraizability hypotheses.

    This is not one yes-or-no assertion. Positive characteristic, singular or unibranch varieties,
nondiscrete valuations, big classes, arbitrary support, and nonalgebraizable analytic spaces
require diﬀerent inputs. The known variational proofs use compactness, envelope regularity,
diﬀerentiability of energy, and a comparison principle; deleting a geometric hypothesis is valid
only after replacing every place where it enters. The relevant positive results and their distinct
domains are surveyed in Book Chapter 28, Book Chapter 29.
    The projectivity axis has one logical constraint. A proper algebraic K-scheme endowed
with an ample line bundle is already projective over K [Stacksb, Tag 0B5N]. Thus P16.2
cannot mean that one retains the BFJ line-bundle polarization L while simply deleting the
word “projective.” A nonprojective proper algebraizable extension must ﬁrst replace that
positivity datum—and then construct the corresponding psh, ﬁnite-energy, and comparison
theory—rather than merely rerun the original argument. No canonical replacement with the
required equation theory is asserted here.
    One exact source-stated axis is especially clean. Pille–Schneider observes that the ﬁnite-
energy space can be deﬁned over an arbitrary non-Archimedean ﬁeld, but that the extension of
the Monge–Ampère operator is not known there in general; the discretely valued characteristic-
zero and trivially valued cases are the established endpoints [PS23, Remark 4.4]. This should
be solved before bundling all remaining axes into a single theorem.

Proposition 10.1 (Arbitrary-ﬁeld invariant toric skeletal endpoint). Let K be a complete
nontrivially valued non-Archimedean ﬁeld, XΣ a proper toric K-variety, and L an ample toric
line bundle. If µ is a positive Radon measure on XΣan , is supported on the canonical skeleton
NΣ , gives zero mass to NΣ \NR , and has total mass degL (XΣ ), then there is a toric continuous
singular psh metric on L whose Monge–Ampère measure is µ. It is unique up to multiplication
of the metric by a positive constant.

    Thus nondiscreteness and the arbitrary complete ground ﬁeld cause no obstruction in
this invariant toric, skeleton-supported range. Here “continuous singular” has the source’s
extended-valued meaning: local weights are continuous into R ∪ {−∞}, as in [BGGJK25,
§5.3.1]. It does not imply ﬁnite real-valued weights or ﬁnite energy. This is not an arbitrary-
ﬁeld ﬁnite-energy theorem in the BFJ sense: the result permits a singular potential, requires
torus invariance and skeletal support, and does not construct the general extended Monge–
Ampère operator. In particular, P16.4 and P16.6 retain the respectively nonskeletal and
noninvariant ﬁnite-energy residual scopes.
    There is also a distinct, nonproper algebraic endpoint. Let n > d ≥ 1, let X be a smooth
projective Fano complex variety of dimension n, and let D be a reduced simple-normal-crossing
anticanonical divisor whose dual complex is the standard (d−1)-simplex. For the aﬃne Calabi–
Yau complement X = X \ D, Wang’s Theorem A constructs a continuous non-Archimedean
psh function on X an , over the trivially valued ﬁeld C, whose local Monge–Ampère measure

                                               74

is the canonical Lebesgue measure on the essential skeleton [Wan25]. The source is a version-
one preprint and uses a local CLD/tropical–convex construction. In particular, it neither
constructs the BFJ ﬁnite-energy operator nor treats arbitrary measures or arbitrary aﬃne
varieties. Since X is aﬃne and hence not proper, this endpoint does not answer P16.2; it
only records a special nonprojective algebraic solution after the properness requirement is
also dropped.
    There is a separate ﬁnite-atomic inverse statement which must not be called a ﬁnite-energy
Monge–Ampère theorem. Under its standing assumptions that K is maximally complete and
|K × | = R>0 , Fang ﬁxes an irreducible projective K-variety with an ample line bundle and a
ﬁnite set of graded birational points on its aﬃne cone. For every probability vector on that
ﬁnite set, the source constructs a Shilov-ﬁnite, possibly singular metric having the prescribed
equidistribution measure [Fan25, Proposition 4.8]. The source itself says that comparing this
Banach-algebra measure with the genuine Monge–Ampère measure requires the separate con-
tinuity property of an envelope metric. Thus it supplies neither a continuous semipositive
solution nor the BFJ ﬁnite-energy operator for the prescribed atomic measure, and does not
narrow P16.6.
    There is also a resolved negative regularity chronology. The ﬁrst skeletal-factorization
question of Gubler–Jell–Künnemann–Martin already fails on their toric surface [GJKM19,
Appendix A]. Boucksom–Jonsson then construct a ﬁnite atomic Monge–Ampère measure sup-
ported on a dual complex whose solution is invariant under no retraction attached to any
SNC model; they also construct a divisorial Green function that is not Q-PL [BJ24b, Theo-
rems A and B]. Hence support on a dual complex does not imply factorization through some
reﬁned skeleton. This is a theorem-level obstruction to a proof strategy, not an open regularity
expectation.
    The Rethlas programme treats each axis separately and ﬁrst searches the post-2020 liter-
ature for an existing theorem. Alterations and universal homeomorphisms can address some
algebraic descent questions, but they do not by themselves supply multiplier ideals or dif-
ferentiability in positive characteristic. The unrestricted formulation is open; several strictly
delimited axes are already known.




                                               75

# Abstract

We establish the retained domain of original P16.1: reduced irreducible geometrically unibranch projective varieties over an arbitrary algebraically closed trivially valued field of characteristic zero, polarized by an actual ample rational line bundle. The conclusion concerns the genuine intersection-theoretic finite-energy Monge--Ampère operator and all positive Radon targets of its intersection mass and finite intrinsic dual energy, with arbitrary support. The new deduction is original-target envelope regularity. We prove the application joining the specified accepted all-point fiber theorem, actual-reference local conversion, geometric witness construction, and repaired countable original-ring affine theorem. First genuine membership on the original variety precedes envelope regularity and every use of onto birational descent. A separate countable field for each finite competitor removes countability. The general-variety energy theory then gives an actually attained variational maximizer and its equation, with both derivative signs. Normalization, mixed products and unbounded limits preserve the original cycle and raw mass.

This is an unverified research draft. Its mathematical premises include exactly the accepted intermediate bodies supplied with the assignment, in the scopes stated below. Their previous acceptance is a task grant, not a claim of a new independent review. The new application and the final theorem are proved here relative to those grants. Compilation and provenance checks have no mathematical force.

# 1. Statement, conventions and premises

Throughout, $k$ is algebraically closed, has characteristic zero, and has the trivial absolute value. There is no countability assumption unless explicitly imposed in Sections 3--5. A variety is reduced and of finite type. The target $X$ is irreducible, geometrically unibranch, and projective over $k$. It may be nonnormal and singular. Its dimension is $n$. The polarization $L$ is an **actual ample rational line bundle**: a positive integral multiple is an honest ample line bundle. Put $\omega=c_1(L)$ and $V=(L^n)>0$. Intersections use the fundamental cycle. A rational bundle is cleared by tensor powers whenever sections or models occur. Analytic spaces and Radon measures are Berkovich spaces and regular Borel measures. Potentials are scalar differences from the canonical trivial metric on the specified bundle, with values in $\mathbb R\cup\{-\infty\}$.

The genuine space $\operatorname{PSH}(X,L)$ is the space of generically finite psh potentials in the sense of Boucksom--Jonsson (BJ). For ample rational $L$, it is the decreasing-net closure of finite Fubini--Study potentials on that same bundle. Its topology is pointwise convergence on divisorial valuations of $k(X)/k$. This topology is called weak below; it is not convergence at every analytic point. Write $\operatorname{PSH}_{\sup}$ for $\sup_X\varphi=0$. For irreducible $X$, the supremum equals the value at the generic trivial valuation. Finite maxima, constants, genuine pullback and decreasing varying-class closure have their usual BJ meanings.

**Theorem 1 (original retained P16.1).** For every $k,X,L$ just specified, $\omega$ has the envelope property, and $\operatorname{PSH}_{\sup}(X,L)$ is compact in the divisorial topology. There are symmetric positive raw mixed Radon measures
$$
 (\omega_1+dd^c\varphi_1)\wedge\cdots\wedge(\omega_n+dd^c\varphi_n)
$$
for actual ample rational $L_i$ and genuine $\varphi_i\in\mathcal E^1(X,L_i)$, of mass $(L_1\cdots L_n)$, continuous along unbounded decreasing nets with genuine finite-energy limits. In particular
$$
 \operatorname{MA}_{m raw,L}(\varphi)=(\omega+dd^c\varphi)^n,
 \qquad \operatorname{MA}_{m raw,L}(\varphi)(X^{m an})=V.
$$
Define
$$
 E_{m raw}(\varphi)= rac{(\omega,\varphi)^{n+1}}{n+1},\quad
 E_{m BJ}=V^{-1}E_{m raw},\quad
 \mathcal E^1(X,L)=\{\varphi\in\operatorname{PSH}(X,L):E_{m raw}(\varphi)>-\infty\}.
$$
Every positive Radon $\mu$ with $\mu(X^{m an})=V$ and
$$
 E_{m raw}^{\vee}(\mu)
 :=\sup_{\varphi\in\mathcal E^1(X,L)}
       \left(E_{m raw}(\varphi)-\int\varphi\,d\muight)<\infty
 	ag{1.1}
$$
has a solution $\varphi_\mu\in\mathcal E^1(X,L)$ of
$$\operatorname{MA}_{m raw,L}(\varphi_\mu)=\mu.$$
It is unique modulo one real constant. Condition (1.1) is equivalent to integrability of **every genuine** $\mathcal E^1(X,L)$ potential against $\mu$. There is no imposed support condition. The raw outer energy satisfies
$$
 \left. rac{d}{dt}ight|_{t=0} E_{m raw}^{\downarrow}(\varphi+tf)
       =\int f\,\operatorname{MA}_{m raw,L}(\varphi)
 	ag{1.2}

Definition 5.8. We say that a class θ ∈ N1 (X) has the envelope property if, for any
bounded-above family (ϕi ) in PSH(θ), the usc upper envelope sup?i ϕi is θ-psh.

satisfy the analogue of the envelope property. As a consequence, θ-psh functions satisfy the

especially delicate. The purpose of what follows is to explore various implications, and

# Abstract

We reconstruct a relative equation theory on every actual big rational line bundle on a smooth integral projective variety over every algebraically closed trivially valued field of characteristic zero. The retained datum is an actual Kodaira decomposition $L=A+D$, with $A$ ample and $D$ effective rational Cartier. The reference is the actual divisor potential $\sigma=\log|s_D|$. We prove that its entire genuine reference-dominated cone is $\sigma+\operatorname{PSH}(A)$, including all points of the divisor. Division is repaired by compactness rather than an incorrect monotonicity assertion about divided approximants. The inverse quotient is a uniquely determined actual psh extension on the original variety. The relative energy is an integral of this quotient against genuine relative metric products. We identify these products first locally, with the correct sign in the frame identity, and then prove their nonpluripolar extension, raw mass $A^n$, unbounded and weighted decreasing limits, comparison, intrinsic target criterion, actual attainment and uniqueness modulo constants. Every continuous direction on the original space is available with both derivative signs. The ample equation is used solely in its exact task-granted actual ample domain.

The additional zero-volume equation proved here is exactly the actual trivial-bundle equation in positive dimension. We distinguish a big blowup with nonpositive self-intersection from a genuinely zero-volume example with noninjective top operator. This is a theorem about prescribed retained Kodaira references, not a class-volume or minimal-singularity theorem, and not a general zero-volume equation. All original big rational bundles occur; no finite-generation, cardinality, invariance or measure-support hypothesis replaces that domain. The conclusion is a mathematical proof draft relative to an explicit task grant and published premises. Evidence processing and compilation do not certify it.

# 1. Statement and the exact retained domain

Let $k$ be algebraically closed, of characteristic zero, with the trivial absolute value. It is complete and may have arbitrary cardinality. Let $X$ be a smooth integral projective $k$-variety of dimension $n\geq1$. Analytification and measures are Berkovich analytification and positive Radon measures. A rational line bundle means an actual element of $\operatorname{Pic}(X)_{\mathbb Q}$, cleared by a common positive integer whenever frames and sections are used. Potentials are scalar differences from the canonical trivial metric. We retain the actual rational-bundle isomorphism
$$
             L\simeq A\otimes\mathcal O_X(D),                  	ag{1.1}
$$
where $A$ is ample and $D$ is effective rational Cartier. This datum is fixed before any measure is specified. Put
$$
 Z=|D|^{m an},\quad U=X^{m an}\setminus Z,\quad
 \sigma=m^{-1}\log\|s_{mD}\|_{m triv},\quad V_D=(A^n)>0.
                                                               	ag{1.2}
$$
The definition of $\sigma$ is independent of the clearing integer. It is finite on $U$, equals $-\infty$ on $Z$, is at most zero, and equals zero at the generic trivial valuation $v_{m triv}$. Every function-field divisorial valuation belongs to $U$ and has finite $\sigma$.

We use the genuine BJ cone $\operatorname{PSH}(X,L)=\operatorname{PSH}(c_1(L))$, not a newly declared cone of formal symbols. It consists of generically finite usc decreasing-net limits of generically finite Fubini--Study potentials in rational classes tending to $c_1(L)$. For an ample actual rational bundle these are decreasing same-class genuine approximants, with the fixed-bundle conversion stated in the task grant. Define the geometric reference cone
$$
 \mathcal P_D(L)=\{u\in\operatorname{PSH}(X,L):u\leq\sigma+C
                                      	ext{ for some }C\in\mathbb R\}. 	ag{1.3}
$$
The topology on this cone is pointwise convergence on function-field divisorial valuations. This is the usual weak psh topology; it is not pointwise convergence at all analytic points.

**Theorem 1 (full big domain with retained divisor reference).** Every actual big rational $L$ on $X$ admits (1.1). For every such datum the map
$$
 F_D:\operatorname{PSH}(X,A)\longrightarrow\mathcal P_D(L),
                 \qquad F_D(\psi)=\sigma+\psi                  	ag{1.4}

     § 8.8. EXTENSION AUX DIFFÉRENCES DE FONCTIONS PSH

Lemme 8.8.1. — Soit u une fonction lisse sur X. Tout point x de X possède un
voisinage sur lequel u s’écrit comme la différence de deux fonctions lisses psh.
   Plus précisément, soit U un ouvert contenu dans un domaine compact W sur lequel u
est tropicalisée par une carte tropicale f , il existe des fonctions lisses psh u1 , u2 sur U ,
f -tropicales, telles que u|U = u1 − u2 .

Démonstration. — Soit f : W → T un moment tropicalisant u, soit P le polyèdre com-
pact f (W ) et soit v une fonction lisse au voisinage de P telle que u|W = v ◦ ftrop .
   D’après la proposition 1.10.2, il existe des fonctions lisses v1 et v2 au voisinage de P
telles que v = v1 −v2 et telles que les formes d′ d′′ v1 et d′ d′′ v2 sont positives. Les fonctions
u1 = v1 ◦ ftrop |U et v2 = u2 ◦ ftrop |U sur U sont lisses, psh, et l’on a u = u1 − u2 .

Proposition 8.8.2. — a) Soit u une fonction G-lisse sur X. Soit W un domaine
analytique compact W sur lequel u est tropicalisée par un moment f , il existe des fonc-
tions convexes v1 , v2 sur l’enveloppe convexe de f (W ) telles que u|U = f ∗ v1 − f ∗ v2 .
   b) Soit u une fonction paralinéaire sur X et soit W un domaine analytique compact
de X sur lequel u est tropicalisée par un moment f . Il existe des fonctions paralinéaires
convexes v1 , v2 sur l’enveloppe convexe de f (W ) telles que u|U = f ∗ v1 − f ∗ v2 .

Démonstration. — D’après la proposition 6.3.4, il existe un voisinage domanial com-
pact V de x, une carte tropicale f : V → E sur V et une fonction G-lisse v sur f (V )
telle que u|V = f ∗ v. Lorsque u est paralinéaire, v l’est. D’après les propositions 1.10.10
et 1.10.11, il existe alors des fonctions convexes v1 et v2 sur l’enveloppe convexe de f (V )
telles que v = v1 − v2 sur f (V ), que l’on peut choisir paralinéaires sur u l’est. D’après la
proposition 8.2.5, les fonctions u1 = f ∗ v1 et u2 = f ∗ v2 sur V sont tropicalement convexes
et sont paralinéaires si u l’est ; elles vérifient u = u1 − u2 .

Corollaire 8.8.3. — Soit u une fonction G-lisse sur X. Tout point de X en lequel X
est décent possède un voisinage sur lequel u s’écrit comme la différence de deux fonctions
tropicalement convexes, que l’on peut choisir paralinéaires si u l’est.

    "literal": "Proposition 28.27.13. Let $X$ be a quasi-compact scheme. Let $\mathcal{L}$ be an invertible sheaf on $X$. Set $S = \Gamma _*(X, \mathcal{L})$. The following are equivalent: 
  
  
 $\mathcal{L}$ is ample, 


 the open sets $X_ s$, with $s \in S_{+}$ homogeneous, cover $X$ and the associated morphism $X \to \text{Proj}(S)$ is an open immersion, 


 the open sets $X_ s$, with $s \in S_{+}$ homogeneous, form a basis for the topology of $X$, 


 the open sets $X_ s$, with $s \in S_{+}$ homogeneous, which are affine form a basis for the topology of $X$, 


 for every quasi-coherent sheaf $\mathcal{F}$ on $X$ the sum of the images of the canonical maps 


  \[  \Gamma (X, \mathcal{F} \otimes _{\mathcal{O}_ X} \mathcal{L}^{\otimes n}) \otimes _{\mathbf{Z}} \mathcal{L}^{\otimes -n} \longrightarrow \mathcal{F}  \]


 with $n \geq 1$ equals $\mathcal{F}$, 


 same property as (5) with $\mathcal{F}$ ranging over all quasi-coherent sheaves of ideals, 


 $X$ is quasi-separated and for every quasi-coherent sheaf $\mathcal{F}$ of finite type on $X$ there exists an integer $n_0$ such that $\mathcal{F} \otimes _{\mathcal{O}_ X} \mathcal{L}^{\otimes n}$ is globally generated for all $n \geq n_0$, 


 $X$ is quasi-separated and for every quasi-coherent sheaf $\mathcal{F}$ of finite type on $X$ there exist integers $n > 0$, $k \geq 0$ such that $\mathcal{F}$ is a quotient of a direct sum of $k$ copies of $\mathcal{L}^{\otimes - n}$, and 


 same as in (8) with $\mathcal{F}$ ranging over all sheaves of ideals of finite type on $X$. 




    
      Proof.
      Lemma 28.27.11 is (1) $\Rightarrow $ (2). Lemmas 28.27.2 and 28.27.12 provide the implication (1) $\Leftarrow $ (2). The implications (2) $\Rightarrow $ (4) $\Rightarrow $ (3) are clear from Constructions, Section 27.8. Lemma 28.27.6 is (3) $\Rightarrow $ (1). Thus we see that the first 4 conditions are all equivalent. 
    
      Assume the equivalent conditions (1) – (4). Note that in particular $X$ is separated (as an open subscheme of the separated scheme $\text{Proj}(S)$). Let $\mathcal{F}$ be a quasi-coherent sheaf on $X$. Choose $s \in S_{+}$ homogeneous such that $X_ s$ is affine. We claim that any section $m \in \Gamma (X_ s, \mathcal{F})$ is in the image of one of the maps displayed in (5) above. This will imply (5) since these affines $X_ s$ cover $X$. Namely, by Lemma 28.18.2 we may write $m$ as the image of $m' \otimes s^{-n}$ for some $n \geq 1$, some $m' \in \Gamma (X, \mathcal{F} \otimes \mathcal{L}^{\otimes n})$. This proves the claim. 
    
      Clearly (5) $\Rightarrow $ (6). Let us assume (6) and prove $\mathcal{L}$ is ample. Pick $x \in X$. Let $U \subset X$ be an affine open which contains $x$. Set $Z = X \setminus U$. We may think of $Z$ as a reduced closed subscheme, see Schemes, Section 26.12. Let $\mathcal{I} \subset \mathcal{O}_ X$ be the quasi-coherent sheaf of ideals corresponding to the closed subscheme $Z$. By assumption (6), there exists an $n \geq 1$ and a section $s \in \Gamma (X, \mathcal{I} \otimes \mathcal{L}^{\otimes n})$ such that $s$ does not vanish at $x$ (more precisely such that $s \not\in \mathfrak m_ x \mathcal{I}_ x \otimes \mathcal{L}_ x^{\otimes n}$). We may think of $s$ as a section of $\mathcal{L}^{\otimes n}$. Since it clearly vanishes along $Z$ we see that $X_ s \subset U$. Hence $X_ s$ is affine, see Lemma 28.27.4. This proves that $\mathcal{L}$ is ample. At this point we have proved that (1) – (6) are equivalent. 
    
      Assume the equivalent conditions (1) – (6). In the following we will use the fact that the tensor product of two sheaves of modules which are globally generated is globally generated without further mention (see Modules, Lemma 17.4.3). By (1) we can find elements $s_ i \in S_{d_ i}$ with $d_ i \geq 1$ such that $X = \bigcup _{i = 1, \ldots , n} X_{s_ i}$. Set $d = d_1\ldots d_ n$. It follows that $\mathcal{L}^{\otimes d}$ is globally generated by 
    
      
  \[  s_1^{d/d_1}, \ldots , s_ n^{d/d_ n}.  \]

    
       This means that if $\mathcal{L}^{\otimes j}$ is globally generated then so is $\mathcal{L}^{\otimes j + dn}$ for all $n \geq 0$. Fix a $j \in \{ 0, \ldots , d - 1\} $. For any point $x \in X$ there exists an $n \geq 1$ and a global section $s$ of $\mathcal{L}^{j + dn}$ which does not vanish at $x$, as follows from (5) applied to $\mathcal{F} = \mathcal{L}^{\otimes j}$ and ample invertible sheaf $\mathcal{L}^{\otimes d}$. Since $X$ is quasi-compact there we may find a finite list of integers $n_ i$ and global sections $s_ i$ of $\mathcal{L}^{\otimes j + dn_ i}$ which do not vanish at any point of $X$. Since $\mathcal{L}^{\otimes d}$ is globally generated this means that $\mathcal{L}^{\otimes j + dn}$ is globally generated where $n = \max \{ n_ i\} $. Since we proved this for every congruence class mod $d$ we conclude that there exists an $n_0 = n_0(\mathcal{L})$ such that $\mathcal{L}^{\otimes n}$ is globally generated for all $n \geq n_0$. At this point we see that if $\mathcal{F}$ is globally generated then so is $\mathcal{F} \otimes \mathcal{L}^{\otimes n}$ for all $n \geq n_0$. 
    
      We continue to assume the equivalent conditions (1) – (6). Let $\mathcal{F}$ be a quasi-coherent sheaf of $\mathcal{O}_ X$-modules of finite type. Denote $\mathcal{F}_ n \subset \mathcal{F}$ the image of the canonical map of (5). By construction $\mathcal{F}_ n \otimes \mathcal{L}^{\otimes n}$ is globally generated. By (5) we see $\mathcal{F}$ is the sum of the subsheaves $\mathcal{F}_ n$, $n \geq 1$. By Modules, Lemma 17.9.7 we see that $\mathcal{F} = \sum _{n = 1, \ldots , N} \mathcal{F}_ n$ for some $N \geq 1$. It follows that $\mathcal{F} \otimes \mathcal{L}^{\otimes n}$ is globally generated whenever $n \geq N + n_0(\mathcal{L})$ with $n_0(\mathcal{L})$ as above. We conclude that (1) – (6) implies (7). 
    
      Assume (7). Let $\mathcal{F}$ be a quasi-coherent sheaf of $\mathcal{O}_ X$-modules of finite type. By (7) there exists an integer $n \geq 1$ such that the canonical map 
    
      
  \[  \Gamma (X, \mathcal{F} \otimes _{\mathcal{O}_ X} \mathcal{L}^{\otimes n}) \otimes _{\mathbf{Z}} \mathcal{L}^{\otimes -n} \longrightarrow \mathcal{F}  \]

    
       is surjective. Let $I$ be the set of finite subsets of $\Gamma (X, \mathcal{F} \otimes _{\mathcal{O}_ X} \mathcal{L}^{\otimes n})$ partially ordered by inclusion. Then $I$ is a directed partially ordered set. For $i = \{ s_1, \ldots , s_{r(i)}\} $ let $\mathcal{F}_ i \subset \mathcal{F}$ be the image of the map 
    
      
  \[  \bigoplus \nolimits _{j = 1, \ldots , r(i)} \mathcal{L}^{\otimes -n} \longrightarrow \mathcal{F}  \]

    
       which is multiplication by $s_ j$ on the $j$th factor. The surjectivity above implies that $\mathcal{F} = \mathop{\mathrm{colim}}\nolimits _{i \in I} \mathcal{F}_ i$. Hence Modules, Lemma 17.9.7 applies and we conclude that $\mathcal{F} = \mathcal{F}_ i$ for some $i$. Hence we have proved (8). In other words, (7) $\Rightarrow $ (8). 
    
      The implication (8) $\Rightarrow $ (9) is trivial. 
    
      Finally, assume (9). Let $\mathcal{I} \subset \mathcal{O}_ X$ be a quasi-coherent sheaf of ideals. By Lemma 28.23.3 (this is where we use the condition that $X$ be quasi-separated) we see that $\mathcal{I} = \mathop{\mathrm{colim}}\nolimits _\alpha I_\alpha $ with each $I_\alpha $ quasi-coherent of finite type. Since by assumption each of the $I_\alpha $ is a quotient of negative tensor powers of $\mathcal{L}$ we conclude the same for $\mathcal{I}$ (but of course without the finiteness or boundedness of the powers). Hence we conclude that (9) implies (6). This ends the proof of the proposition. 
      $\square$

    "literal": "Lemma 30.16.1. Let $R$ be a Noetherian ring. Let $X \to \mathop{\mathrm{Spec}}(R)$ be a proper morphism. Let $\mathcal{L}$ be an ample invertible sheaf on $X$. Let $\mathcal{F}$ be a coherent $\mathcal{O}_ X$-module. 
  
  
The graded ring $A = \bigoplus _{d \geq 0} H^0(X, \mathcal{L}^{\otimes d})$ is a finitely generated $R$-algebra. 


There exists an $r \geq 0$ and $d_1, \ldots , d_ r \in \mathbf{Z}$ and a surjection 


  \[  \bigoplus \nolimits _{j = 1, \ldots , r} \mathcal{L}^{\otimes d_ j} \longrightarrow \mathcal{F}.  \]


For any $p$ the cohomology group $H^ p(X, \mathcal{F})$ is a finite $R$-module. 


If $p > 0$, then $H^ p(X, \mathcal{F} \otimes _{\mathcal{O}_ X} \mathcal{L}^{\otimes d}) = 0$ for all $d$ large enough. 


For any $k \in \mathbf{Z}$ the graded $A$-module 


  \[  \bigoplus \nolimits _{d \geq k} H^0(X, \mathcal{F} \otimes _{\mathcal{O}_ X} \mathcal{L}^{\otimes d})  \]


 is a finite $A$-module. 




    
      Proof.
      By Morphisms, Lemma 29.40.4 there exists a $d > 0$ and an immersion $i : X \to \mathbf{P}^ n_ R$ such that $\mathcal{L}^{\otimes d} \cong i^*\mathcal{O}_{\mathbf{P}^ n_ R}(1)$. Since $X$ is proper over $R$ the morphism $i$ is a closed immersion (Morphisms, Lemma 29.42.7). Thus we have $H^ i(X, \mathcal{G}) = H^ i(\mathbf{P}^ n_ R, i_*\mathcal{G})$ for any quasi-coherent sheaf $\mathcal{G}$ on $X$ (by Lemma 30.2.4 and the fact that closed immersions are affine, see Morphisms, Lemma 29.11.10). Moreover, if $\mathcal{G}$ is coherent, then $i_*\mathcal{G}$ is coherent as well (Lemma 30.9.8). We will use these facts without further mention. 
    
      Proof of (1). Set $S = R[T_0, \ldots , T_ n]$ so that $\mathbf{P}^ n_ R = \text{Proj}(S)$. Observe that $A$ is an $S$-algebra (but the ring map $S \to A$ is not a homomorphism of graded rings because $S_ n$ maps into $A_{dn}$). By the projection formula (Cohomology, Lemma 20.54.2) we have 
    
      
  \[  i_*(\mathcal{L}^{\otimes nd + q}) = i_*(\mathcal{L}^{\otimes q}) \otimes _{\mathcal{O}_{\mathbf{P}^ n_ R}} \mathcal{O}_{\mathbf{P}^ n_ R}(n)  \]

    "literal": "Lemma 33.45.1. Let $k$ be a field. Let $X$ be a proper scheme over $k$. Let $\mathcal{F}$ be a coherent $\mathcal{O}_ X$-module. Let $\mathcal{L}_1, \ldots , \mathcal{L}_ r$ be invertible $\mathcal{O}_ X$-modules. The map 
  
  \[  (n_1, \ldots , n_ r) \longmapsto \chi (X, \mathcal{F} \otimes \mathcal{L}_1^{\otimes n_1} \otimes \ldots \otimes \mathcal{L}_ r^{\otimes n_ r})  \]

   is a numerical polynomial in $n_1, \ldots , n_ r$ of total degree at most the dimension of the support of $\mathcal{F}$. 

    
      Proof.
      We prove this by induction on $\dim (\text{Supp}(\mathcal{F}))$. If this number is zero, then the function is constant with value $\dim _ k \Gamma (X, \mathcal{F})$ by Lemma 33.33.3. Assume $\dim (\text{Supp}(\mathcal{F})) > 0$. 
    
      If $\mathcal{F}$ has embedded associated points, then we can consider the short exact sequence $0 \to \mathcal{K} \to \mathcal{F} \to \mathcal{F}' \to 0$ constructed in Divisors, Lemma 31.4.6. Since the dimension of the support of $\mathcal{K}$ is strictly less, the result holds for $\mathcal{K}$ by induction hypothesis and with strictly smaller total degree. By additivity of the Euler characteristic (Lemma 33.33.2) it suffices to prove the result for $\mathcal{F}'$. Thus we may assume $\mathcal{F}$ does not have embedded associated points. 
    
      If $i : Z \to X$ is a closed immersion and $\mathcal{F} = i_*\mathcal{G}$, then we see that the result for $X$, $\mathcal{F}$, $\mathcal{L}_1, \ldots , \mathcal{L}_ r$ is equivalent to the result for $Z$, $\mathcal{G}$, $i^*\mathcal{L}_1, \ldots , i^*\mathcal{L}_ r$ (since the cohomologies agree, see Cohomology of Schemes, Lemma 30.2.4). Applying Divisors, Lemma 31.4.7 we may assume that $X$ has no embedded components and $X = \text{Supp}(\mathcal{F})$. 
    
      Pick a regular meromorphic section $s$ of $\mathcal{L}_1$, see Divisors, Lemma 31.26.4. Let $\mathcal{I} \subset \mathcal{O}_ X$ be the ideal of denominators of $s$ and consider the maps 
    
      
  \[  \mathcal{I}\mathcal{F} \to \mathcal{F},\quad \mathcal{I}\mathcal{F} \to \mathcal{F} \otimes \mathcal{L}_1  \]

    
       of Divisors, Lemma 31.25.5. These are injective and have cokernels $\mathcal{Q}$, $\mathcal{Q}'$ supported on nowhere dense closed subschemes of $X = \text{Supp}(\mathcal{F})$. Tensoring with the invertible module $\mathcal{L}_1^{\otimes n_1} \otimes \ldots \otimes \mathcal{L}_ r^{\otimes n_ r}$ is exact, hence using additivity again we see that 
    
      
  \begin{align*} & \chi (X, \mathcal{F} \otimes \mathcal{L}_1^{\otimes n_1} \otimes \ldots \otimes \mathcal{L}_ r^{\otimes n_ r}) - \chi (X, \mathcal{F} \otimes \mathcal{L}_1^{\otimes n_1 + 1} \otimes \ldots \otimes \mathcal{L}_ r^{\otimes n_ r}) \\ &  = \chi (\mathcal{Q} \otimes \mathcal{L}_1^{\otimes n_1} \otimes \ldots \otimes \mathcal{L}_ r^{\otimes n_ r}) - \chi (\mathcal{Q}' \otimes \mathcal{L}_1^{\otimes n_1} \otimes \ldots \otimes \mathcal{L}_ r^{\otimes n_ r}) \end{align*}

    
       Thus we see that the function $P(n_1, \ldots , n_ r)$ of the lemma has the property that 
    
      
  \[  P(n_1 + 1, n_2, \ldots , n_ r) - P(n_1, \ldots , n_ r)  \]

    
       is a numerical polynomial of total degree $<$ the dimension of the support of $\mathcal{F}$. Of course by symmetry the same thing is true for 
    
      
  \[  P(n_1, \ldots , n_{i - 1}, n_ i + 1, n_{i + 1}, \ldots , n_ r) - P(n_1, \ldots , n_ r)  \]

    
       for any $i \in \{ 1, \ldots , r\} $. A simple arithmetic argument shows that $P$ is a numerical polynomial of total degree at most $\dim (\text{Supp}(\mathcal{F}))$. 
      $\square$

    "literal": "Lemma 30.18.1. Let $S$ be a Noetherian scheme. Let $f : X \to S$ be a separated morphism of finite type. Then there exist an $n \geq 0$ and a diagram 
  
  \[  \xymatrix{ X \ar[rd] &  X' \ar[d] \ar[l]^\pi \ar[r] &  \mathbf{P}^ n_ S \ar[dl] \\  &  S &  }  \]

   where $X' \to \mathbf{P}^ n_ S$ is an immersion, and $\pi : X' \to X$ is proper and surjective. Moreover, we may arrange it such that there exists a dense open subscheme $U \subset X$ such that $\pi ^{-1}(U) \to U$ is an isomorphism. 

    
      Proof.
      All of the schemes we will encounter during the rest of the proof are going to be of finite type over the Noetherian scheme $S$ and hence Noetherian (see Morphisms, Lemma 29.15.6). All morphisms between them will automatically be quasi-compact, locally of finite type and quasi-separated, see Morphisms, Lemma 29.15.8 and Properties, Lemmas 28.5.4 and 28.5.8. 
    
      The scheme $X$ has only finitely many irreducible components (Properties, Lemma 28.5.7). Say $X = X_1 \cup \ldots \cup X_ r$ is the decomposition of $X$ into irreducible components. Let $\eta _ i \in X_ i$ be the generic point. For every point $x \in X$ there exists an affine open $U_ x \subset X$ which contains $x$ and each of the generic points $\eta _ i$. See Properties, Lemma 28.30.4. Since $X$ is quasi-compact, we can find a finite affine open covering $X = U_1 \cup \ldots \cup U_ m$ such that each $U_ i$ contains $\eta _1, \ldots , \eta _ r$. In particular we conclude that the open $U = U_1 \cap \ldots \cap U_ m \subset X$ is a dense open. This and the fact that the $U_ i$ are affine opens covering $X$ are all that we will use below. 
    
      Let $X^* \subset X$ be the scheme theoretic closure of $U \to X$, see Morphisms, Definition 29.6.2. Let $U_ i^* = X^* \cap U_ i$. Note that $U_ i^*$ is a closed subscheme of $U_ i$. Hence $U_ i^*$ is affine. Since $U$ is dense in $X$ the morphism $X^* \to X$ is a surjective closed immersion. It is an isomorphism over $U$. Hence we may replace $X$ by $X^*$ and $U_ i$ by $U_ i^*$ and assume that $U$ is scheme theoretically dense in $X$, see Morphisms, Definition 29.7.1. 
    
      By Morphisms, Lemma 29.40.3 we can find an immersion $j_ i : U_ i \to \mathbf{P}_ S^{n_ i}$ for each $i$. By Morphisms, Lemma 29.7.7 we can find closed subschemes $Z_ i \subset \mathbf{P}_ S^{n_ i}$ such that $j_ i : U_ i \to Z_ i$ is a scheme theoretically dense open immersion. Note that $Z_ i \to S$ is proper, see Morphisms, Lemma 29.44.5. Consider the morphism 
    
      
  \[  j = (j_1|_ U, \ldots , j_ m|_ U) : U \longrightarrow \mathbf{P}_ S^{n_1} \times _ S \ldots \times _ S \mathbf{P}_ S^{n_ m}.  \]

    
       By the lemma cited above we can find a closed subscheme $Z$ of $\mathbf{P}_ S^{n_1} \times _ S \ldots \times _ S \mathbf{P}_ S^{n_ m}$ such that $j : U \to Z$ is an open immersion and such that $U$ is scheme theoretically dense in $Z$. The morphism $Z \to S$ is proper. Consider the $i$th projection 
    
      
  \[  \text{pr}_ i|_ Z : Z \longrightarrow \mathbf{P}^{n_ i}_ S.  \]

    
       This morphism factors through $Z_ i$ (see Morphisms, Lemma 29.6.6). Denote $p_ i : Z \to Z_ i$ the induced morphism. This is a proper morphism, see Morphisms, Lemma 29.42.7 for example. At this point we have that $U \subset U_ i \subset Z_ i$ are scheme theoretically dense open immersions. Moreover, we can think of $Z$ as the scheme theoretic image of the “diagonal” morphism $U \to Z_1 \times _ S \ldots \times _ S Z_ m$. 
    
      Set $V_ i = p_ i^{-1}(U_ i)$. Note that $p_ i|_{V_ i} : V_ i \to U_ i$ is proper. Set $X' = V_1 \cup \ldots \cup V_ m$. By construction $X'$ has an immersion into the scheme $\mathbf{P}^{n_1}_ S \times _ S \ldots \times _ S \mathbf{P}^{n_ m}_ S$. Thus by the Segre embedding (see Constructions, Lemma 27.13.6) we see that $X'$ has an immersion into a projective space over $S$. 
    
      We claim that the morphisms $p_ i|_{V_ i}: V_ i \to U_ i$ glue to a morphism $X' \to X$. Namely, it is clear that $p_ i|_ U$ is the identity map from $U$ to $U$. Since $U \subset X'$ is scheme theoretically dense by construction, it is also scheme theoretically dense in the open subscheme $V_ i \cap V_ j$. Thus we see that $p_ i|_{V_ i \cap V_ j} = p_ j|_{V_ i \cap V_ j}$ as morphisms into the separated $S$-scheme $X$, see Morphisms, Lemma 29.7.10. We denote the resulting morphism $\pi : X' \to X$. 
    
      We claim that $\pi ^{-1}(U_ i) = V_ i$. Since $\pi |_{V_ i} = p_ i|_{V_ i}$ it follows that $V_ i \subset \pi ^{-1}(U_ i)$. Consider the diagram 
    
      
  \[  \xymatrix{ V_ i \ar[r] \ar[rd]_{p_ i|_{V_ i}} &  \pi ^{-1}(U_ i) \ar[d] \\  &  U_ i }  \]

    
       Since $V_ i \to U_ i$ is proper we see that the image of the horizontal arrow is closed, see Morphisms, Lemma 29.42.7. Since $V_ i \subset \pi ^{-1}(U_ i)$ is scheme theoretically dense (as it contains $U$) we conclude that $V_ i = \pi ^{-1}(U_ i)$ as claimed. 
    
      This shows that $\pi ^{-1}(U_ i) \to U_ i$ is identified with the proper morphism $p_ i|_{V_ i} : V_ i \to U_ i$. Hence we see that $X$ has a finite affine covering $X = \bigcup U_ i$ such that the restriction of $\pi $ is proper on each member of the covering. Thus by Morphisms, Lemma 29.42.3 we see that $\pi $ is proper. 
    
      Finally we have to show that $\pi ^{-1}(U) = U$. To see this we argue in the same way as above using the diagram 
    
      
  \[  \xymatrix{ U \ar[r] \ar[rd] &  \pi ^{-1}(U) \ar[d] \\  &  U }  \]

    
       and using that $\text{id}_ U : U \to U$ is proper and that $U$ is scheme theoretically dense in $\pi ^{-1}(U)$. 
      $\square$

    "literal": "Lemma 37.53.6. Let $f : X \to S$ be a morphism of schemes. Assume 
  
  
$f$ is proper, 


$S$ is integral with generic point $\xi $, 


$S$ is normal, 


$X$ is reduced, 


every generic point of an irreducible component of $X$ maps to $\xi $, 


we have $H^0(X_\xi , \mathcal{O}) = \kappa (\xi )$. 



   Then $f_*\mathcal{O}_ X = \mathcal{O}_ S$ and $f$ has geometrically connected fibres. 

    
      Proof.
      Apply Theorem 37.53.5 to get a factorization $X \to S' \to S$. It is enough to show that $S' = S$. This will follow from Morphisms, Lemma 29.55.8. Namely, $S'$ is reduced because $X$ is reduced (Morphisms, Lemma 29.54.8). The morphism $S' \to S$ is integral by the theorem cited above. Every generic point of $S'$ lies over $\xi $ by Morphisms, Lemma 29.54.9 and assumption (5). On the other hand, since $S'$ is the relative spectrum of $f_*\mathcal{O}_ X$ we see that the scheme theoretic fibre $S'_\xi $ is the spectrum of $H^0(X_\xi , \mathcal{O})$ which is equal to $\kappa (\xi )$ by assumption. Hence $S'$ is an integral scheme with function field equal to the function field of $S$. This finishes the proof. 
      $\square$

    "literal": "Lemma 33.17.3. Let $X$ be a Noetherian scheme. Let $f : Y \to X$ be a birational proper morphism of schemes with $Y$ reduced. Let $U \subset X$ be the maximal open over which $f$ is an isomorphism. Then $U$ contains 
  
  
every point of codimension $0$ in $X$, 


every $x \in X$ of codimension $1$ on $X$ such that $\mathcal{O}_{X, x}$ is a discrete valuation ring, 


every $x \in X$ such that the fibre of $Y \to X$ over $x$ is finite and such that $\mathcal{O}_{X, x}$ is normal, and 


every $x \in X$ such that $f$ is quasi-finite at some $y \in Y$ lying over $x$ and $\mathcal{O}_{X, x}$ is normal. 




    
      Proof.
      Part (1) follows from Morphisms, Lemma 29.52.6. Part (2) follows from part (3) and Lemma 33.17.2 (and the fact that finite morphisms have finite fibres). 
    
      Part (3) follows from part (4) and Morphisms, Lemma 29.21.7 but we will also give a direct proof. Let $x \in X$ be as in (3). By Cohomology of Schemes, Lemma 30.21.2 we may assume $f$ is finite. We may assume $X$ affine. This reduces us to the case of a finite birational morphism of Noetherian affine schemes $Y \to X$ and $x \in X$ such that $\mathcal{O}_{X, x}$ is a normal domain. Since $\mathcal{O}_{X, x}$ is a domain and $X$ is Noetherian, we may replace $X$ by an affine open of $x$ which is integral. Then, since $Y \to X$ is birational and $Y$ is reduced we see that $Y$ is integral. Writing $X = \mathop{\mathrm{Spec}}(A)$ and $Y = \mathop{\mathrm{Spec}}(B)$ we see that $A \subset B$ is a finite inclusion of domains having the same field of fractions. If $\mathfrak p \subset A$ is the prime corresponding to $x$, then $A_\mathfrak p$ being normal implies that $A_\mathfrak p \subset B_\mathfrak p$ is an equality. Since $B$ is a finite $A$-module, we see there exists an $a \in A$, $a \not\in \mathfrak p$ such that $A_ a \to B_ a$ is an isomorphism. 
    
      Let $x \in X$ and $y \in Y$ be as in (4). After replacing $X$ by an affine open neighbourhood we may assume $X = \mathop{\mathrm{Spec}}(A)$ and $A \subset \mathcal{O}_{X, x}$, see Properties, Lemma 28.30.8. Then $A$ is a domain and hence $X$ is integral. Since $f$ is birational and $Y$ is reduced it follows that $Y$ is integral too. Consider the ring map $\mathcal{O}_{X, x} \to \mathcal{O}_{Y, y}$. This is a ring map which is essentially of finite type, the residue field extension is finite, and $\dim (\mathcal{O}_{Y, y}/\mathfrak m_ x\mathcal{O}_{Y, y}) = 0$ (to see this trace through the definitions of quasi-finite maps in Morphisms, Definition 29.21.1 and Algebra, Definition 10.122.3). By Algebra, Lemma 10.124.2 $\mathcal{O}_{Y, y}$ is the localization of a finite $\mathcal{O}_{X, x}$-algebra $B$. Of course we may replace $B$ by the image of $B$ in $\mathcal{O}_{Y, y}$ and assume that $B$ is a domain with the same fraction field as $\mathcal{O}_{Y, y}$. Then $\mathcal{O}_{X, x} \subset B$ have the same fraction field as $f$ is birational. Since $\mathcal{O}_{X, x}$ is normal, we conclude that $\mathcal{O}_{X, x} = B$ (because finite implies integral), in particular, we see that $\mathcal{O}_{X, x} = \mathcal{O}_{Y, y}$. By Morphisms, Lemma 29.43.4 after shrinking $X$ we may assume there is a section $X \to Y$ of $f$ mapping $x$ to $y$ and inducing the given isomorphism on local rings. Since $X \to Y$ is closed (by Schemes, Lemma 26.21.11) necessarily maps the generic point of $X$ to the generic point of $Y$ it follows that the image of $X \to Y$ is $Y$. Then $Y = X$ and we've proved what we wanted to show. 
      $\square$

    "literal": "Proposition 28.27.13. Let $X$ be a quasi-compact scheme. Let $\mathcal{L}$ be an invertible sheaf on $X$. Set $S = \Gamma _*(X, \mathcal{L})$. The following are equivalent: 
  
  
 $\mathcal{L}$ is ample, 


 the open sets $X_ s$, with $s \in S_{+}$ homogeneous, cover $X$ and the associated morphism $X \to \text{Proj}(S)$ is an open immersion, 


 the open sets $X_ s$, with $s \in S_{+}$ homogeneous, form a basis for the topology of $X$, 


 the open sets $X_ s$, with $s \in S_{+}$ homogeneous, which are affine form a basis for the topology of $X$, 


 for every quasi-coherent sheaf $\mathcal{F}$ on $X$ the sum of the images of the canonical maps 


  \[  \Gamma (X, \mathcal{F} \otimes _{\mathcal{O}_ X} \mathcal{L}^{\otimes n}) \otimes _{\mathbf{Z}} \mathcal{L}^{\otimes -n} \longrightarrow \mathcal{F}  \]


 with $n \geq 1$ equals $\mathcal{F}$, 


 same property as (5) with $\mathcal{F}$ ranging over all quasi-coherent sheaves of ideals, 


 $X$ is quasi-separated and for every quasi-coherent sheaf $\mathcal{F}$ of finite type on $X$ there exists an integer $n_0$ such that $\mathcal{F} \otimes _{\mathcal{O}_ X} \mathcal{L}^{\otimes n}$ is globally generated for all $n \geq n_0$, 


 $X$ is quasi-separated and for every quasi-coherent sheaf $\mathcal{F}$ of finite type on $X$ there exist integers $n > 0$, $k \geq 0$ such that $\mathcal{F}$ is a quotient of a direct sum of $k$ copies of $\mathcal{L}^{\otimes - n}$, and 


 same as in (8) with $\mathcal{F}$ ranging over all sheaves of ideals of finite type on $X$. 




    
      Proof.
      Lemma 28.27.11 is (1) $\Rightarrow $ (2). Lemmas 28.27.2 and 28.27.12 provide the implication (1) $\Leftarrow $ (2). The implications (2) $\Rightarrow $ (4) $\Rightarrow $ (3) are clear from Constructions, Section 27.8. Lemma 28.27.6 is (3) $\Rightarrow $ (1). Thus we see that the first 4 conditions are all equivalent. 
    
      Assume the equivalent conditions (1) – (4). Note that in particular $X$ is separated (as an open subscheme of the separated scheme $\text{Proj}(S)$). Let $\mathcal{F}$ be a quasi-coherent sheaf on $X$. Choose $s \in S_{+}$ homogeneous such that $X_ s$ is affine. We claim that any section $m \in \Gamma (X_ s, \mathcal{F})$ is in the image of one of the maps displayed in (5) above. This will imply (5) since these affines $X_ s$ cover $X$. Namely, by Lemma 28.18.2 we may write $m$ as the image of $m' \otimes s^{-n}$ for some $n \geq 1$, some $m' \in \Gamma (X, \mathcal{F} \otimes \mathcal{L}^{\otimes n})$. This proves the claim.

We may think of $Z$ as a reduced closed subscheme, see Schemes, Section 26.12. Let $\mathcal{I} \subset \mathcal{O}_ X$ be the quasi-coherent sheaf of ideals corresponding to the closed subscheme $Z$. By assumption (6), there exists an $n \geq 1$ and a section $s \in \Gamma (X, \mathcal{I} \otimes \mathcal{L}^{\otimes n})$ such that $s$ does not vanish at $x$ (more precisely such that $s \not\in \mathfrak m_ x \mathcal{I}_ x \otimes \mathcal{L}_ x^{\otimes n}$). This proves that $\mathcal{L}$ is ample. At this point we have proved that (1) – (6) are equivalent. 
    
      Assume the equivalent conditions (1) – (6). In the following we will use the fact that the tensor product of two sheaves of modules which are globally generated is globally generated without further mention (see Modules, Lemma 17.4.3). By (1) we can find elements $s_ i \in S_{d_ i}$ with $d_ i \geq 1$ such that $X = \bigcup _{i = 1, \ldots , n} X_{s_ i}$. Set $d = d_1\ldots d_ n$. It follows that $\mathcal{L}^{\otimes d}$ is globally generated by 
    
      
  \[  s_1^{d/d_1}, \ldots , s_ n^{d/d_ n}.  \]

    
       This means that if $\mathcal{L}^{\otimes j}$ is globally generated then so is $\mathcal{L}^{\otimes j + dn}$ for all $n \geq 0$. Fix a $j \in \{ 0, \ldots , d - 1\} $. For any point $x \in X$ there exists an $n \geq 1$ and a global section $s$ of $\mathcal{L}^{j + dn}$ which does not vanish at $x$, as follows from (5) applied to $\mathcal{F} = \mathcal{L}^{\otimes j}$ and ample invertible sheaf $\mathcal{L}^{\otimes d}$. Since $\mathcal{L}^{\otimes d}$ is globally generated this means that $\mathcal{L}^{\otimes j + dn}$ is globally generated where $n = \max \{ n_ i\} $. Since we proved this for every congruence class mod $d$ we conclude that there exists an $n_0 = n_0(\mathcal{L})$ such that $\mathcal{L}^{\otimes n}$ is globally generated for all $n \geq n_0$. # An actual proper nonprojective test over every retained field

Root continuation111, 5 October2026. This is a new unreviewed supplement
to the original-domain P16.2 proposal109 and conditional continuation110.
It does not close P16.2. The active native author109 and review108 have
not received this supplement, and their private outputs were not read.

## 1. Attribution and exact fan

The seven-ray example below is the Miyake--Oda example, as reproduced in
Fujino--Sato, *Smooth projective toric varieties whose nontrivial nef line
bundles are big*, Proc. Japan Acad.85A(2009), Example4.4, printed pages92--93.
It is not a new example. The downloaded author's PDF was inspected on
PDF page4 to recover signs that its literal text extraction loses.

For any field k let N=Z^3 and put

    v1=(1,0,0), v2=(0,1,0), v3=(0,0,1),
    v4=(-1,-1,-1), v5=(0,-1,-1),
    v6=(-1,0,-1), v7=(-1,-1,0).

Take all faces of the maximal cones

    123, 125, 256, 456, 236, 367, 467, 137, 157, 457.

Here ijk means the nonnegative real span of vi,vj,vk. This agrees exactly
with the rays and ten maximal cones printed in Example4.4. The primary
source supplies attribution and an independent check of the example.
The verifications below avoid restricting its construction to C.

## 2. Completeness and smoothness

Start with the P^3 fan whose maximal cones are 123,124,234,134.
The first cone is unchanged. On each of the other three cones, place the
two rays along its edges from v4 and choose the following subdivisions:

    124 -> 125,256,456,
    234 -> 236,367,467,
    134 -> 137,157,457.

For a basis (a,b,c) of an original cone, the first pattern has new rays
a+c,b+c and consists of (a,b,a+c), (b,a+c,b+c), (c,a+c,b+c).
Its triangular cross-section is triangulated by these three triangles,
so they cover that cone and meet along faces. The next two patterns are
cyclic copies. On every shared face of the old P^3 fan, both subdivisions
use precisely the same new edge ray. They therefore glue to a fan with
the same support R^3. This proves completeness.

The determinants of the three displayed new basis matrices are,
respectively, 1,-1,1 times det(a,b,c). Every old maximal cone has
determinant +/-1. Thus each new maximal cone is generated by a Z-basis.
Its affine chart Spec k[sigma^vee intersect M] is A^3_k. These charts cover
X_Sigma(k), proving smoothness over any k directly. They contain the same
dense Laurent torus, so the glued scheme is integral and has dimension3.

For properness over any k, the primary input is Rohrer's dissertation,
ChapterIV, Lemma1.3.11 and Theorem1.3.12, with their entire printed
proofs. The theorem is over any ring R: a nonempty fan gives a proper
toric scheme if and only if the fan is complete (apart from R=0).
The proof of the sufficient direction is not a complex-topological
compactness argument. Given a DVR point whose generic point lies in
the orbit of a cone sigma, valuation of its character homomorphism is a
lattice vector in N/(N intersect span sigma). Completeness of the star
fan supplies a chart where all required character values have nonnegative
valuation, hence lie in the DVR. The valuative criterion first proves
properness over Z; base change proves it over every R.

The pertinent orbit-cover proof is IV1.3.1--1.3.9, also read. The star
completeness statement and printed proof are II2.2.5--2.2.7, read separately.
For clarity a direct proof of the only star-completeness implication used
is as follows. For z in relint(sigma) and any x in N_R, completeness gives
a cone containing z+epsilon_j x for a sequence epsilon_j decreasing to0.
Finiteness gives a single such cone tau for infinitely many j. Its closedness
gives z in tau, and the fan face property then gives sigma face of tau.
Projecting z+epsilon_j x shows that the image of x lies in tau/sigma.
Consequently the star fan covers the quotient real vector space.

The dissertation's IV1.2.1 gives separatedness, quasi-compactness and
finite presentation. Its printed proof cites earlier lemmas; reading those
earlier lemma proofs is not asserted here. The use of Theorem1.3.12 is
an exact external theorem with an inspected main proof and the listed
pertinent orbit/star units, not a claim that every foundation in the
249-page dissertation has been read. Rohrer1207.0605v2 and the survey
1107.2713v2 only refer elsewhere for properness; neither survey statement
is represented as a printed properness proof.

## 3. A direct nonprojectivity proof in every field

Any line bundle on X has a rational section trivializing its restriction
to the Laurent torus: the Laurent polynomial ring is a UFD, hence the
Picard group of its regular spectrum is zero. The section's divisor is
supported on the complement of that torus, so it has the form

    D=sum_{i=1}^7 a_i D_i,

with integer coefficients and invariant boundary prime divisors D_i.
Since X is smooth, this is a Cartier divisor. Thus checking the degree
of every invariant Cartier divisor suffices to exclude all ample bundles.

The walls 25,36,17 have the respective wall relations

    v1+v6=v2+v5,
    v2+v7=v3+v6,
    v3+v5=v1+v7.

The associated invariant orbit closures are P^1_k. To see this and the
degree formula without importing an intersection table, write adjacent
basis cones as (w1,w2,v) and (w1,w2,v') with v+v'=w1+w2. Quotienting
the orbit by the two wall coordinates glues A^1_z and A^1_{z^-1}.
Let e in M vanish on w1,w2 with e(v)=1, so e(v')=-1.
The monomial frames of O(D) on these two charts are chi^{m_sigma} and
chi^{m_sigma'}, where the pairings with chart rays equal minus their
divisor coefficients. Their difference vanishes on the wall and satisfies

    m_sigma'-m_sigma=(a_v+a_v'-a_w1-a_w2)e.

The transition of the second frame to the first is therefore z^d, with
d=a_v+a_v'-a_w1-a_w2. A rational section equal to the first frame has
order d at the other chart's origin, proving that its line bundle on
this orbit closure has degree d. Hence the three degrees above are

    d25=a1+a6-a2-a5,
    d36=a2+a7-a3-a6,
    d17=a3+a5-a1-a7.

Their sum is zero. An ample line bundle restricts to an ample bundle
on each of these P^1 curves, hence would have all three degrees positive.
This is impossible. Thus X is proper and smooth but nonprojective over
every field, including every algebraically closed trivially valued
characteristic-zero field retained by the original task.

## 4. Actual positivity data and role of this test

The refinement of the P^3 fan gives a toric morphism pi0:X->P^3 which
is identity on the dense torus. It is proper: X is proper over k and P^3
is separated over k, so its graph is closed and the projection is proper.
It is birational. Normality of P^3 and the actual proper birational
pushforward theorem (Stacks0AY8) give (pi0)_*O_X=O_P3. Projection formula
then gives

    H^0(X,pi0^*O(m))=H^0(P^3,O(m)),

whose dimension grows as binomial(m+3,3). Therefore pi0^*O(1) is an actual
big line bundle on this original nonprojective X. Proposal109 constructs
a retained smooth projective modification pi:Y->X and an ample/effective
decomposition pi^*L=A+D for this bundle, as for every big rational bundle
on every smooth integral proper original carrier.

This example tests the nonprojective part of that proposed general theorem.
No claim restricts the theorem to toric metrics, toric targets, atomic
measures, a fixed skeleton, or the particular projective contraction above.
No proof of the remaining analytic gates is supplied merely by this example.
Those gates, and the conditional continuation110 arguments, still require
their full original-domain reconstruction and independent review.

# Obtaining the retained modification on every original proper carrier

Root continuation112, 5 October2026. This is an unreviewed geometric
application audit for proposal109. It does not certify its analytic
theorem or close original P16.2. Active native109 was not inspected or
given this note as feedback.

Let k be any algebraically closed field of characteristic zero, with its
trivial absolute value, and let X be a smooth integral proper k-variety.
There is no countability or projectivity hypothesis on X or k. Here a
variety is finite type, so the use of noetherian resolution below does
not introduce an extra restriction on the original carrier.

## 1. A projective integral Chow modification

Stacks0200 and0201, in the exact primary units already read and bound for
109, give Chow's lemma for the proper original X. The resulting proper
modification Z->X is an isomorphism over a dense open and has an immersion
into projective space over k. Since Z is proper over k and projective
space is separated over k, this immersion is proper, hence closed. Thus
Z is projective over k. If necessary take the reduced irreducible component
dominating X. It is a closed projective integral subscheme and still
agrees with that original dense open. Denote it again by Z. The morphism
Z->X is actual, proper and birational, rather than an abstract
identification of two function spaces.

## 2. Exact resolution hypotheses

Temkin0904.1592v2, Theorem1.2.1, is stated for noetherian quasi-excellent
generically reduced schemes over Spec(Q). It supplies a finite blowup
sequence, regular centers away from the preimage of the regular locus,
and regular final scheme. The printed main proof and the finite
stabilization Lemma4.1.3 were read in the supplied literal dictionary,
and checked again in the actual downloaded v2 text. This does not assert
that the whole35-page paper or every recursively cited lemma was read.
In particular its variety-resolution algorithm is an external input to
the paper; that background is not a new theorem supplied by this note.

The actual Z satisfies every relevant hypothesis. A field is excellent,
and any finite-type algebra over a field is excellent (Stacks07QW).
Finite-type affine patches of Z are therefore noetherian and
quasi-excellent. Z is integral, hence generically reduced. Characteristic
zero gives its structural map to Spec(Q). There is no need for Z to be
finite type over Q: the theorem asks for quasi-excellence and a map to Q,
and those have just been checked. The field k may have arbitrarily large
transcendence degree and cardinality.

The output Y is regular, integral and finite type over k. Integrality
of each blowup follows by writing the Rees algebra of a nonzero ideal
of an integral ring as a subring of its polynomial ring. The centers
avoid a dense regular open, so each blowup is birational and does not
remove the generic point. A characteristic-zero field is perfect.
Stacks0B8X therefore makes regularity of this finite-type reduced Y
equivalent to smoothness over k. Hence Y is smooth.

Stacks07QU also states preservation of quasi-excellence under localization,
but its printed proof explicitly omits the localization part. That
unprinted proof is not represented as read or needed here: a cover by
finite-type affine k-algebras already suffices for quasi-excellence of Z.
The inspected proof of07QW invokes earlier G-ring and J-2 results; a
reading of their full proofs is not asserted either.

## 3. Why the final scheme is actually projective

The finite sequence in Temkin's definition2.2.1--2.2.2 consists of ordinary
blowups along fixed coherent ideal sheaves. Projectivity can be checked
on the actual projective carrier at every step without assuming that
every proper original X has an ample bundle.

Suppose the current scheme Z_i is projective over k and I is its coherent
center ideal. Choose an ample integral H_i. For a large m, I tensor H_i^m
is globally generated (Stacks01Q3, the previously bound exact global
generation unit). Thus H_i^(-m) direct-sum r surjects onto I for a finite r.
Taking symmetric powers gives a surjection of graded algebras onto the
Rees algebra direct-sum I^j. Relative Proj realizes the blowup as a closed
subscheme of P_{Z_i}(H_i^(-m) direct-sum r), which is isomorphic to
Z_i times P^{r-1}_k. The blowup is therefore projective over k. Empty
centers give the identity and cause no difficulty. Induction through the
finite blowup sequence proves that Y is projective over k.

The composite pi:Y->Z->X is proper and birational. This proves existence
of the smooth projective modification retained by proposal109 for EVERY
smooth integral proper original X under the stated field assumptions.

## 4. The replacement positivity datum is nonempty

For completeness, the subsequent algebraic construction of109 can now
be applied without a hidden projectivity assumption on X. Choose an
effective very ample Cartier divisor H on Y avoiding all exceptional
prime divisors of pi. There are finitely many such primes. Each imposes
a proper linear condition on the finite-dimensional global section space;
their finite union cannot fill it over the infinite field k. Let B=pi_*H.
It is effective Cartier on smooth X. Since a proper birational map onto
normal X is an isomorphism at its codimension-one points (Stacks0BFP),
the strict-transform coefficients of pi^*B equal those of H. The pullback
pi^*B is effective and H contains no exceptional prime, so

    pi^*B=H+E, with E effective and exceptional.

The actual pushforward identity pi_*O_Y=O_X (Stacks0AY8) and the
projection formula identify H^0(X,mB) with H^0(Y,m pi^*B). Multiplication
by the section of mE embeds H^0(Y,mH) in that space. The positive leading
coefficient of the ample Hilbert polynomial proves growth at least c m^n,
so B is a big Cartier line bundle on the actual nonprojective X.

For ANY retained big rational L on X, clearing denominators and applying
the same pushforward identity gives the equality of section spaces for
L and pi^*L, hence pi^*L is big on projective Y. The no-Bertini
hyperplane-restriction proof107 then gives a decomposition pi^*L=A+D
with A ample rational and D effective rational Cartier. That proof uses
finite associated primes and a regular section on a possibly nonreduced
hyperplane, so no unmentioned smooth-hyperplane choice is required.

Consequently the retained data (L,pi:Y->X,A,D) proposed for the
nonprojective axis exist on every carrier and for every actual big L in
the declared domain. Different data remain different equation theories;
no independence of the chosen modification or decomposition is inferred
from this existence proof. Original-carrier psh descent, genuine metric
products, all energy limits, all Radon targets and the actual equation
are separate proof obligations.

## 5. Source and acceptance boundary

The resolution theorem here is the pinned0904.1592v2, dated11 December2011,
not the embedded-boundary paper0912.2570. Its exact statement, the main
proof and the finite stabilization unit were already supplied in the
ample99 primary dictionary; a new application still needs its own
hypothesis assessment, supplied above. Additional source statements
07QW,07QU and0B8X were opened independently on5 October2026. Exact byte
bindings and local extraction coordinates are recorded separately.
This is not a claimed solution of resolution in positive characteristic,
nor a construction on nonalgebraizable analytic spaces.

# Finite fixed-bundle approximants before descending their common poles

Root continuation113, 5 October2026. This is an unreviewed repair of the
single-stage approximation detail in proposal109. It proves that detail
on the retained ample projective Y before adding sigma_D and descending.
It does not prove the converse cone identity or close original P16.2.
Active native109 and review108 have not received this note as feedback.

Retain k,X,Y,pi,L,A,D from109, with A an ACTUAL ample rational line bundle
on projective integral Y and pi^*L=A+D. The original carrier X is allowed
to be nonprojective. The retained field is algebraically closed, trivially
valued, characteristic zero, with no cardinality restriction.

## 1. A finite fixed-A family

Let F_A be the finite real-valued functions on Y^an obtained as actual
Fubini--Study section maxima for A:

    m^(-1) max_i(log ||s_i||_triv + lambda_i),

where mA is an actual integral line bundle and the finite displayed
section family s_i globally generates mA. Constants lambda_i are real.
These functions are continuous real-valued. They are genuine A-psh,
and the family is stable under adding constants and finite maxima.
For different m's, clear to a common multiple and raise the respective
sections to powers before taking their union. This preserves each
function and global generation.

The function0 belongs to F_A. Choose a globally generating family of
sections of some mA. Each has norm at most1 everywhere in the canonical
trivial metric: at the valuative center it is a regular coefficient of
a local frame of norm1. At every analytic point at least one generator
is a unit at that center, hence has norm1. The maximum logarithmic norm
is therefore exactly0. The valuative-center description is BJ1.24 on
the retained proper projective Y; it is not asserted on a hypothetical
ample bundle on nonprojective X.

For any actual nonzero s in H^0(Y,mA), put a=m^(-1)log ||s||_triv.
Clearing to a sufficiently divisible globally generated power of A,
the function max(a,-j) is in F_A: combine a raised copy of s with a
globally generating family of weight corresponding to the constant-j.
It decreases pointwise to a, including every zero of s. Thus every
single section logarithm used in BJ4.18 is a decreasing limit of
FINITE fixed-A approximants.

## 2. The finite family's single-stage decreasing closure is stable

Let D_A consist of generically finite pointwise limits of decreasing nets
from F_A. Addition of constants and finite maxima preserve D_A; for
maxima take the product of the two directed indices. We prove directly
that decreasing limits of elements of D_A stay in D_A. This uses the
compact flattening argument behind BJ4.6 only with finite continuous
inner functions.

Suppose psi_i decreases to a generically finite psi, and each psi_i is
the decreasing limit of f_{i,j} in F_A. Use indices alpha=(i,j,epsilon),
epsilon>0, and order them by

    alpha>=alpha' iff i>=i' and
                     f_{i,j}+epsilon <= f_{i',j'}+epsilon' everywhere.

This is directed. For two indices, choose i3 above both outer indices
and epsilon3 smaller than both positive epsilons. We have

    psi_i3+epsilon3 < min(f_i1,j1+epsilon1, f_i2,j2+epsilon2)

at EVERY point. The upper functions are finite, so this remains a
strict inequality where psi_i3 is minus infinity. The continuous
real-valued functions

    exp(f_i3,j+epsilon3)
       -exp(min(f_i1,j1+epsilon1, f_i2,j2+epsilon2))

decrease to a strictly negative function pointwise. Their negative open
sets increase to a cover of compact Y^an. A finite subcover and
directedness of j give one j3 for which the displayed inequality holds
globally. This provides an index above both original indices.

Now g_alpha=f_{i,j}+epsilon lies in F_A and is a decreasing net, bounded
below pointwise by psi. At any point with finite psi value, first choose
an outer i0 whose psi_i0 value is close enough to psi, then an inner j0
and epsilon0 whose g_alpha0 value is arbitrarily close from above.
Every subsequent index remains below it. At a point with psi=-infinity,
use an arbitrary real threshold instead. Thus g_alpha decreases to psi
at every point, proving stability of D_A under decreasing limits.

The restriction to finite inner approximants is useful: if both upper
approximants have a common minus-infinity value, the attempted strict
inequality -infinity+epsilon < -infinity+epsilon' is false. We do not
use that step on original L-section maxima with their common D poles.
This argument is a direct restricted proof and makes no claim that all
extended-valued families satisfy a flattening argument without further
care at their common poles.

BJ4.18 identifies PSH(Y,A) with the smallest non-identically-minus-infinity
class containing the actual A-section logarithms and stable under
constants, finite maxima and decreasing limits. Sections1--2 therefore
give

    D_A=PSH(Y,A).

The reverse inclusion also uses the genuine psh stability of decreasing
generically finite limits. No countable extraction was made; this is a
single net on the actual fixed rational line bundle A.

## 3. Literal original sections after clearing denominators

Fix psi in PSH(Y,A) and choose the finite fixed-A net psi_i above.

section degree to a common positive integer p. Raise its A-sections to
the appropriate powers and multiply each by the canonical section of

Every resulting section is thus the pullback of an actual original

pullback of an actual original section maximum u_i, with exactly the

with c1(L_i) tending to theta. This defining single net is an input to
the definition, not a consequence of the false general flattening lemma.
No varying-class decreasing closure theorem is used below.

## 1. Rational coefficients directly within the defining net

Let phi_i=m_i^(-1)max_j(log||s_ij||+lambda_ij), where lambda_ij are real.
For every delta>0 round each of this finite family's coefficients upward
to a rational coefficient with error at most m_i delta. Denote the
result by f_i,delta. It is an actual rational-coefficient FS function
in the SAME actual L_i and satisfies, at every point,

    phi_i <= f_i,delta <= phi_i+delta.

At a common zero both sides are minus infinity and these non-strict
inequalities remain valid. Now put g_i,delta=f_i,delta+delta, taking
positive rational delta so g_i,delta still has rational coefficients.
Order pairs by i>=i' and g_i,delta<=g_i',delta' everywhere. This is
directed: choose i3 above two given i's and rational delta3 with
2delta3<=min(delta1,delta2). Then

    g_i3,delta3 <= phi_i3+2delta3
               <= min(phi_i1,phi_i2)+min(delta1,delta2)
               <= min(g_i1,delta1,g_i2,delta2).

All inequalities also hold at common poles. The resulting g-net decreases
pointwise to phi: first choose i approximating its desired point value,
then delta small; at a minus-infinity value use an arbitrary finite
threshold. Its line-bundle classes still tend to theta because the
pair order refines the original i order. This gives genuine rational
FS approximation directly. No compact strict-shift argument or nested
decreasing closure is needed.

## 2. Every such numerical function lies in a fixed actual ample cone

Choose an actual rational ample H with c1(H)-theta ample. Eventually
the ACTUAL rational bundle H-L_i is ample. A generating family of a
sufficiently divisible power of H-L_i has logarithmic section maximum0
in the canonical trivial metric. Multiply the sections representing
phi_i by these generators after clearing degrees. The resulting actual
H-section maximum is identically phi_i. Hence the defining decreasing
tail is a fixed actual-H net, and phi belongs to the genuine ample
PSH(X,H) cone.

Consequently the ample grant supplies finite divisorial values, generic
maximum, all-point divisorial determination, and the implication from
divisorial inequalities to any usc obstacle for every numerical phi in
this definition. This application does not need a nonample
regularization or closure theorem. Different theta's may require
different H's. Finite groups of functions can be placed in one H by
taking it sufficiently positive.

## 3. Direct homogeneous approximation

For a function phi with nonnegative generic maximum define

    hat(phi)(v)=inf_{t>0} phi(t v)/t,

where scaling t v scales the valuation and keeps its support. This
operator preserves pointwise order. If phi_i decreases to phi, then

    inf_i hat(phi_i)(v)
      =inf_i inf_t phi_i(t v)/t
      =inf_t inf_i phi_i(t v)/t
      =hat(phi)(v).

The two infima commute for arbitrary directed nets and extended values.
Each approximant can be chosen rational by Section1, still with
nonnegative generic maximum. For

    phi=m^(-1)max_j(log||s_j||+lambda_j), lambda_j rational,

hat(phi) is an ACTUAL homogeneous FS section maximum in the same
rational bundle. Here is the finite-dimensional proof. For finite real
x_j and max lambda_j>=0,

    inf_{r>=0} max_j(x_j+r lambda_j)
      =max_{w in W} sum_j w_j x_j,

where W is the finite set of vertices of

    {w_j>=0, sum w_j=1, sum w_j lambda_j>=0}.

One can verify the equality without a general duality black box. Each
weighted expression is at most the displayed max for every r. A
minimum of that convex piecewise-linear function occurs at r=0, at a
breakpoint with active slopes of opposite signs, or is its limit as
r tends to infinity. At r=0 choose an active nonnegative slope. At an
interior minimum take weights on two active slopes with weighted slope0.
In the final case max lambda=0 and choose an active zero slope. These
are vertices of the displayed polytope and give equality. Its vertices
are unit vectors of nonnegative slope, and the two-slope zero averages;
all weights are rational for rational lambda.

Clear a common denominator b of these finitely many w's. The monomials
product_j s_j^(b w_j) are sections of mbL. Their logarithmic maximum
divided by mb is exactly hat(phi). Coefficients zero in a monomial
mean that its corresponding section is absent from the product. The
same formula holds if some x_j=-infinity: replace them by max(x_j,-N),
commute the two infima over N and r, and pass through the fixed finite
maximum of products. Thus it includes all base-locus points.

The generic value of hat(phi_i) is0. The homogeneous functions decrease
to hat(phi); their actual bundle classes converge to theta. Therefore
hat(phi) is genuine by the original definition. If h is already
homogeneous, hat(h)=h. This proves exactly the nonample homogeneous
approximation required in draft105, without BJ4.15 or BJ4.6.

## 4. Direct decomposition by homogeneous components

For an arbitrary genuine phi with C=phi(v_triv), put

    h_lambda=hat(phi-lambda), lambda<C.

Section3 makes h_lambda a genuine homogeneous theta-psh function with
generic value0. Taking t=1 gives h_lambda+lambda<=phi. At every actual
point v we claim

    phi(v)=sup_{lambda<C}(h_lambda(v)+lambda).

The proof is one-dimensional. Along its scaling ray put g(t)=phi(t v).
Each defining FS approximant is convex and decreasing in t>0 and is
bounded above by its generic value. Its decreasing limit g is either
finite convex on (0,infinity), or identically minus infinity there.
Indeed a minus-infinity value forces minus infinity at all smaller t
by convexity with a finite upper-bound point, and then at all larger t
by monotonicity. The identically-minus-infinity case gives the asserted
formula immediately.

In the finite case, choose a supporting line a t+lambda0 at t=1.
The slope is nonpositive and its intercept lambda0 is at most C:
evaluate at t approaching0 and use g(t)<=C. If lambda0<C, then
h_lambda0(v)>=a and the formula follows from equality at t=1. If
lambda0=C, lower its intercept by epsilon>0. Then
h_(C-epsilon)(v)>=a and the resulting expression is at least
g(1)-epsilon. Let epsilon decrease to0. Together with the opposite
inequality h_lambda+lambda<=phi, this proves the formula at every
point, including singular-support points.

Only elementary convexity and the definition enter this proof. It
does not import the unproved varying-class closure behind BJ6.24.

## 5. The actual fixed-divisor cone follows from ample compactness

Literal section division now needs no closure argument. At each

    "literal": "2.1.6. Due to Remark 2.1.7, this does not assume dependency on Hironaka’s paper.
2.1.14. Categories. In this paper, we denote by QE the category of generically
reduced noetherian qe schemes and by QE reg its subcategory containing only regular
morphisms. Of main interest for our needs are the full subcategories Varp=0,reg and
QE p=0,reg of QE reg . The objects in Varp=0,reg are ﬁnite disjoint unions of generically
reduced varieties of characteristic zero and the objects of QE p=0,reg are generically
reduced noetherian qe schemes over Q. The reason to consider disjoint unions of
varieties deﬁned over diﬀerent ﬁelds will become clear in §2.3.5.
2.2. Blow up sequences.
 10                                MICHAEL TEMKIN


2.2.1. Blow ups. Basic facts about blow ups can be found in [Tem1, §2.1] or in
the literature cited there. Recall that the blow up f : BlV (X) → X along a closed
subscheme V is the universal morphism such that f ∗ (V ) := V ×X BlV (X) is a
Cartier divisor. We will use the terminology of [Tem1] with one important excep-
tion: when we say that Y → X is a blow up (or Y is a blow up of X), we always
mean that the center V of the blow up is ﬁxed. So, strictly speaking, we always
mean (usually implicitly) that an isomorphism Y f   →BlV (X) is ﬁxed. The reason
for this change is that we will study functoriality, and the choice of V increases
canonicity of constructions, see, for example, §2.2.6. Following the convention of
[Kol] we call a blow up Bl∅ (X)f  →X empty or trivial blow up. This is the only
blow up we will sometimes ignore. However, even empty blow ups play important
synchronizing role when patching local desingularizations, see §§2.3.4–2.3.6. Note
that though any blow up along a Cartier divisor induces an isomorphism on the
level of schemes, it may play a non-trivial role for functorial desingularization. In
our case this is mainly the synchronization (similarly to empty blow up), but in the
embedded case such blow ups induce non-trivial operations of strict and controlled
transforms, so they cannot be ignored by no means.

2.2.2. Blow up sequences. A price one has to pay for using a ﬁner notion of blow ups
is that the composition X ′′ → X ′ → X of blow ups cannot be considered as a blow
up in a natural way: though X ′′ → X is isomorphic to a blow up BlW (X) → X, it
is not clear how to choose W canonically. Therefore we deﬁne a blow up sequence

of length n to be a composition of n ≥ 0 blow ups Xn → · · · → X1 → X0 with
centers Vi ֒→ Xi . In particular, a blow up sequence of length 0 is just the object
X0 itself. Such sequence is called empty. It will be convenient to denote a blow up
sequence as f : Xn 99K X0 and say that Vi ’s are its centers. We stress that a blow
up sequence is not deﬁned by the morphism Xn → X even when we blow up regular
schemes along regular centers, see [Kol, 3.33]. A sequence will be called contracted
if all its blow ups are non-empty. Using dashed arrows we will sometimes split blow
up sequences, e.g. f : Xn 99K Xi+1 → Xi 99K X0 .

2.2.3. Equality/isomorphism of blow up sequences. An isomorphism between two
blow up sequences Xn′ 99K X0 and Xn 99K X0 is a set of isomorphisms Xi′ f      →Xi
which identify X0 ’s and the centers. Obviously, if two blow up sequences of X are

slight abuse of language that two such blow up sequences are equal, and this cannot
cause any confusion. For example, this agreement allows us to say ”unique” in
Lemma 2.2.1 below instead of ”unique up to unique isomorphism”.
